facts.fact: Name for the term: "omnivores"
Name for the term: "omnivorous"
Name for the term: "Cá ăn tạp"
Name for the term: "loài ăn tạp"
Omnivores need a diet that includes both meat and plants.
Most aquarium fish are omnivores.
Most ornamental fish are omnivores; fish can be split into three groups: algae eaters, predators and omnivores.
Omnivores are the easiest fish to feed and can eat both predators' and algae eaters' foods.
Omnivores are very flexible in their diet.
Fish that graze periphyton and also chase live prey are omnivores, including livebearers (swordtails, platys, guppies, mollies), barbs, gouramis and bettas.
Bottom feeders such as catfish, loaches and carp are also called omnivores, or more technically limnivores; goldfish, which eat anything, are omnivores too.
Almost all grazers are technically omnivores; there are no true herbivores in the aquarium hobby.
At a basic level a keeper can at least determine whether a fish is carnivorous, omnivorous or herbivorous, but protein and lipid requirements beyond that are unknown.
Wild guppies (Poecilia reticulata) eat algal remains, diatoms, invertebrates, zooplankton and detritus, with algal remains usually the biggest share.
Some guppy varieties (Poecilia reticulate, as the page writes it), such as Gold Tuxedo and Koi Red Ear, are omnivores that eat many kinds of food.
A balanced diet is a staple food supplemented with frozen, freeze-dried or live foods.
Omnivores can be fed dry foods (flakes, pellets for bottom fish), chopped boiled vegetables (cabbage, cucumber, lettuce) and live foods (artemia, insects, mosquito larvae).
Omnivores can be fed a varied mix of dry, live and prepared foods.
Vegetables such as zucchini, cucumber and pumpkin suit omnivores and plant-eaters; boil them lightly without salt or oil.
Feeding a wide variety of feeds, including live feeds combined with commercial feeds, helps meet nutritional needs and keeps fish from eating only one feed.
Adult fish are fed about 3% of body weight daily for maintenance; fry and fingerlings up to 5%.
Most aquarium fish should be fed at least daily.
Food should be more than 30% protein and less than 50% carbohydrate by dry weight; juveniles benefit from at least 40% (preferably over 50%) protein and at least 10% fat.
Bottom-dwellers should get rapidly sinking foods and surface feeders floating foods.
Guppies should get commercial food combined with varied live foods, fed in small amounts split into several meals a day.
Split the day's food into several small meals rather than one large feeding.
Keep dry feed in a pest-proof container in a cool, low-humidity place; heat and humidity degrade it, promote mould and mycotoxins and cause rancidity.
Discard dry feed kept at room temperature 2 months after opening, commercial frozen feeds after 6 months, and frozen brine shrimp, bloodworms, mysids or glassworms after 1 year.
Expecting bottom-dwellers such as loricariids and Corydoras catfish to live on other fish's leftovers is not acceptable; they need targeted feeding.
Assuming one fish's diet suits a similar but unrelated species is dangerous.
Refreezing thawed feeds is a mistake.
Thawing frozen food and refreezing the leftovers is a mistake.
Because omnivores eat almost anything, including rice, keepers easily feed them wrongly.
Rice has little nutrition and much starch that fish digest poorly; feeding much of it can cause digestive upset and over time kill fish.
Rice should only be a stopgap; for omnivores such as guppies and mollies it can be given about twice a week.
Goldfish have no stomach and are especially affected by being fed rice often.
Feeding poultry feed to ornamental fish is a mistake because of its high salt and unsuitable additives.
Both overfeeding and underfeeding harm fish.
Overfeeding is the top cause of tank pollution, and vegetables left in the tank over 12 hours dirty the water.
Leftover food in the tank pollutes the water.
Neighbours feeding the fish while the owner is away may overfeed them.
Omnivores do not need a high-protein diet, according to this Vietnamese shop article.
Aquarium Science says it is wrong that omnivores or herbivores need different diets from carnivores; tropical fish of all these types do not need differing diets.
Aquarium Science says grazers are not solely vegetable eaters; they eat a lot of animal protein.
Aquarium Science says it is false that grazers bloat from high protein; bloat is more likely linked to high carbohydrates and low roughage.
Aquarium Science says plant proteins like soy are not equal to periphyton protein: soy lacks two essential amino acids, while periphyton is a complete protein.
Hepatic lipidosis can result from starvation, a high percentage of carbohydrates, high lipids or rancid feed.
Lack of dietary vitamin C causes 'broken back disease', with severe scoliosis and deformed gill cartilage; fish need ascorbic acid in their feed.
